direct_claims: This chart compares global biomass, measured in tonnes of carbon, with the abundance of organisms, measured as number of individuals, across different taxonomic groups.
The chart belongs to the biodiversity and global ecology domain.
The axes are logarithmic, indicating that the comparison spans many orders of magnitude rather than small linear differences.
The chart is branded by Our World in Data and cites Bar-On, Phillips, and Milo (2018) as the data source.
In ecology, biomass reflects the total mass of living material, here standardized as carbon mass, while abundance counts individuals; these are related but distinct measures.
Because the axes are logarithmic, equal spacing represents multiplicative changes, so taxa separated by one major tick differ by about an order of magnitude.
The chart states that these are order-of-magnitude estimates, so the intended takeaway is broad scale and relative comparison rather than exact ranking at fine precision.
derived_claims: The purpose appears to be to show that the most numerous forms of life are not necessarily the ones contributing the most total biomass. — derived from comparing relative positions of taxa across abundance and biomass axes.

Plants appear to have very high biomass despite much lower abundance than microbial groups such as bacteria, archaea, and viruses. — derived from reading relative placement of plants versus microbes on both axes.
Viruses appear extremely abundant but contribute much less biomass than bacteria or plants. — derived from reading virus position as far right but relatively low on biomass axis.

A group can have huge abundance but modest biomass if its members are individually very small, as suggested by viruses and microbial taxa on this chart. — derived from contrasting high abundance with lower biomass positions for viruses and microbes.

Conversely, a group can have lower abundance but very large biomass if individuals are large or long-lived, as suggested by plants. — derived from contrasting plant biomass position with its lower abundance position.

Bacteria appear among the highest in abundance and also among the highest in biomass, implying that they are both numerous and collectively substantial in carbon mass. — derived from reading bacterial position relative to other taxa.

Fungi and protists appear to occupy an intermediate pattern: very large biomass and abundance, but below bacteria in abundance and below plants in biomass. — derived from comparing fungi and protists to bacteria and plants.

Marine arthropods, annelids, cnidarians, fish, humans, and wild birds occupy much lower abundance ranges than microbial groups and generally lower biomass ranges than plants, bacteria, and fungi. — derived from comparing labeled positions across taxa.

This chart matters because it shows that human intuition about which organisms dominate Earth can be misleading if domination is defined by biomass rather than by visibility or familiarity. — derived from comparing positions of familiar animal groups with plants and microbes.
It suggests that plants, bacteria, fungi, and other less visible groups are central to the planet's living carbon distribution. — derived from identifying taxa occupying highest biomass regions.

The relatively small position of humans in biomass compared with many other taxa suggests that human influence on Earth is not mainly through our own biomass but through our ecological and technological impacts. — derived from comparing human biomass position with larger taxa groups.

The chart also highlights why microbes are fundamental to biogeochemical cycles: some microbial groups combine enormous abundance with substantial biomass. — derived from reading microbial abundance and biomass positions.

The image alone does not provide enough information to recover uncertainty ranges or methodological caveats for each taxonomic estimate. — derived from absence of uncertainty annotations or detailed methods in the image.
speculative_claims: Interpreting the chart correctly requires recognizing that taxonomic groups differ greatly in typical body size, life history, and how an 'individual' is counted. — source: ecology.

This has implications for conservation and ecosystem management, because protecting ecosystem function may depend heavily on preserving high-biomass and high-turnover groups, not only charismatic animals. — source: conservation biology.

The relatively small position of humans in biomass compared with many other taxa suggests that human influence on Earth is not mainly through our own biomass but through our ecological and technological impacts. — source: environmental science.
The chart also highlights why microbes are fundamental to biogeochemical cycles: some microbial groups combine enormous abundance with substantial biomass. — source: microbiology.

If such distributions were altered substantially by land-use change, climate change, pollution, or biodiversity loss, the consequences could extend to carbon cycling, food webs, and ecosystem resilience. — source: Earth system science.
